analysis.one_liner: Bans internet providers from blocking, slowing, or charging websites for faster delivery.
analysis.headline: The net neutrality bill from the 112th Congress was introduced in January 2011, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and never received a vote or a hearing action before the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have written net neutrality rules into law: internet providers could not block, slow down, or favor some websites over others, could not charge websites extra for faster delivery, and could not force customers to buy bundled phone or cable TV service to get internet access. It also set up ways for customers and state attorneys general to sue providers who broke the rules. The bill was introduced by Senator Maria Cantwell with one cosponsor, Senator Al Franken, and was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it stayed without any further action for the rest of the Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users, small websites, startups, and consumers who would gain enforceable protections against internet providers blocking or slowing sites, charging websites for priority delivery, or bundling internet with phone and cable service.

how_it_helps.text: Bars broadband providers from blocking, interfering with, or degrading a user's access to lawful content, applications, or services, and from blocking the use of legal devices of the user's choice.
Prohibits pay-for-priority schemes in which providers charge websites or services for faster or prioritized delivery, and bars discrimination or preference for a provider's own affiliated services.
Requires providers to offer stand-alone broadband service without forcing customers to buy phone or cable TV service as a condition, and directs the FCC to write rules enforcing this within 180 days.

Creates an expedited FCC complaint process resolved within 90 days, allows private lawsuits for full damages plus attorney's fees, and lets state attorneys general sue to enforce the rules or seek civil penalties.
Requires providers to publicly disclose network management practices, performance, and commercial terms in plain language so consumers can make informed choices.

analysis.who_pays: Broadband internet providers — cable, telephone, and wireless companies — which would lose the ability to charge websites for priority delivery, favor their own services, or require bundled purchases; they would bear compliance and potential liability costs.

drawbacks.text: Reasonable network management is allowed but only under a strict presumption: it must be essential, narrowly tailored, and the least restrictive option available, which could make legitimate traffic management like network congestion control legally riskier for providers.
The bill allows the FCC to exempt competitively sensitive or security-related information from disclosure, so some provider practices could remain hidden from consumers.
Private lawsuits and state enforcement against providers for the full amount of damages plus attorney's fees would expose companies to potentially broad litigation risk.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver strong consumer protections at a cost mainly to broadband providers, who could no longer charge websites for faster lanes or require bundling. The strict 'reasonable network management' presumption and broad private and state enforcement rights are aggressive and could generate litigation over routine network operations, but the core protections target practices providers are unlikely to defend as beneficial to users.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in January 2011 and never advanced past committee before the 112th Congress ended, so it never received a vote in either chamber.

narrative.text: Senator Maria Cantwell introduced the bill on January 25, 2011, with Senator Al Franken as a cosponsor.
After introduction, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action was taken on the bill for the remainder of the 112th Congress, which ended January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband providers like cable and telephone companies benefited because the bill never advanced, leaving them free of statutory net neutrality obligations and without exposure to private suits or state enforcement under its terms.

for.name: Sen. Maria Cantwell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured its referral to the Senate Commerce Committee.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action for the rest of the Congress, keeping it from reaching the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: Only two senators, both Democrats, are recorded in support; no votes were held and no opposition is documented in the record.

industries.industry: Broadband internet providers (cable, telephone, and wireless)
industries.note: The bill would bar these companies from blocking or slowing websites, charging sites for priority delivery, favoring their own affiliated services, or forcing customers into bundles — practices that were a potential revenue source and a way to steer customers toward their own offerings.
